activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these versions are called isotopes, but they always have the same number of protons.
story:
Thomas had exactly forty minutes before the bus left, so he could postpone the gift shop only so long. He stood in front of the giant periodic table painted on the science museum wall, hunting for one thing: carbon. When he found C in the fourth box down, two numbers waited there. He remembered what Mr. Luo had drilled into them before the trip, that the smaller number, the atomic number, told you the protons, so carbon had six protons. Six. He said it under his breath like a password.

Then a guide's voice drifted over from the next exhibit, where a display case held a bone and a label reading carbon-14. "That bone is dated using carbon-14," the guide said. A little kid near the front raised his hand. "If it's fourteen, why is it carbon? Fourteen isn't six."

Thomas felt the same question open up in his own head, like a door swinging inward. Fourteen. Six. Something did not fit, and he wanted to know what.

He remembered sitting in Mr. Luo's classroom two weeks earlier, the week before the trip was almost postponed by a snowstorm. Mr. Luo had drawn a lopsided atom on the whiteboard, a cluster in the middle and dots orbiting it, and asked the class, "Can you see an atom? No. So how do you know it's there?" Haroun had said, "Because stuff behaves like it's there," and Mr. Luo had grinned and erased the board without another word. Thomas had walked home that day turning the question over. Maybe that was the trick, to believe in a rule you could not see and test whether things fit it.

Knox elbowed him now. "You're doing your thinking face." Thomas pointed at the display. "Carbon is six protons. So what's the fourteen?" Knox shrugged and wandered toward the interactive screen nearby, and Thomas followed. The screen showed a slider that added small grey balls, neutrons, to a cluster of six red ones. When he dragged the slider to eight grey balls, the label changed: carbon-14. He slid it back to seven: carbon-13. Carbon-12. The red six never moved.

"So the fourteen is neutrons plus protons," Knox said slowly, watching the grey balls pile up. "Different carbons." Thomas nodded, feeling his pulse tick faster, the way it did at the climax of a mystery when the pieces snapped together. "But they're all still carbon, because the protons stay six. It's the most logical thing," he said. He looked back at the bone in the case, then at the little kid still waiting near the guide, and called over, "Hey, it's still carbon! Six protons, just extra neutrons."

"Those versions are called isotopes," the guide said.

Thomas slid the neutron slider up, then down, watching the red six hold steady. "Huh," he said. "Neutrons are the flexible ones."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers know who is receiving the real treatment, so their expectations cannot sway the results.
story:
Paige had until eight o'clock tomorrow morning to build a science fair project that actually worked, and the pharmacy on Maple Street was her last stop before closing. She grabbed a basket and went down the cold aisle, hunting for the two brands of cough syrup she needed for her taste test. Her project had collapsed that afternoon when Eshal pointed out the flaw.

"You poured the samples yourself, Paige," Eshal had said on the bus. "You knew which cup was which. When you smiled at Jackson, he probably guessed you wanted him to like the cheap one."

"He said both tasted like cherry poison," Paige protested, but she knew Eshal was right. Jackson had laughed and picked the expensive brand anyway, and now her whole data table was useless.

At the pharmacy counter she found Ms. Marino, the pharmacist, checking a shelf of vitamins. Paige asked whether the store had plain syrup, the kind with no medicine in it, so she could mix it herself and make the samples truly identical except for price.

"You're doing what the big drug trials do," Ms. Marino said, sliding a bottle toward her. "They call it double-blind."

"Double-blind," Paige repeated.

"Neither the participants nor the researchers know who is receiving the real treatment," Ms. Marino said, ringing it up. "So nobody's expectations can sway the results." Then she turned to the next customer, and Paige stood there holding the bottle, turning the idea over.

It was almost like her grandmother's story, the one she told every winter, about how honey and lemon cured her cough in three days when nothing else worked. Paige had always believed it, partly out of empathy, because her grandmother had suffered through those nights. But one person getting better could mean the cough would have ended anyway. A trial where nobody knew who got what, not even the person handing out the cups, that was something you could actually trust.

She called Eshal from the sidewalk. "New plan. You mix the samples tonight and label them with numbers only you know. Tomorrow you hand them out, and neither of us tells Jackson anything."

"That's radical," Eshal said. "You're cutting yourself out of your own experiment."

"It's the only way the data will sustain a conclusion," Paige said. "Meet me at the gym at seven with the cups."

She ran the last two blocks home, syrup bottle rattling in her backpack, already rewriting the headings on her poster board. In her head she heard Eshal's voice: numbers only you know. Paige smiled and wrote it down.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A traditional formal outline labels main points with Roman numerals such as I, II and III, and the details under each point with capital letters such as A and B.
story:
Joseph had one goal for the writing club meeting: finish his outline so he could start drafting his essay about why the school should have a lacrosse team. The essay contest deadline was Friday, and he did not dread much in life, but he dreaded turning in a messy paper more than he dreaded dodge ball, and that was saying something.

"Your thesis has to state your position in one sentence," Ms. Moose said, walking between the desks. "Then three main points supporting it. Outline first, draft second."

Joseph stared at his blank page. Kya leaned over from the next desk. "What's your thesis?"

"That our school needs a lacrosse team," Joseph said. "Point one, not enough spring sports. Point two, we already have a field. Point three, equipment is cheaper than people think."

"Solid," said Clarke, spinning his pencil. "Now label it. Main points get Roman numerals like I, II and III. Details under each point get capital letters like A and B."

"Roman numerals?" said a small voice from the doorway. It was Joseph's little brother, waiting to walk home with him. "Those look like the numbers on a clock."

Joseph laughed. "They are the same numbers, just drawn with letters." He started his outline. He wrote his thesis at the top, then I for his first main point. Under it went A, more spring sports options, and B, kids who quit track need something new. II got the field argument, with A and B under that too. His first real outline, a kind of prototype for the whole essay, and it looked almost competent.

Then came the twist. When he read it back, he noticed something strange. His best point, the cheap equipment one, was hiding under III-B as a detail, when really it deserved to be a whole main point. The outline had shown him a problem he couldn't see when the ideas were just loose in his head. He tried moving it up to II and suddenly his argument flowed in a better order, strong point, strong point, quick point.

"Ms. Moose," Joseph called. "Can I rearrange my Roman numerals before I draft?"

She looked at his page and smiled. "That's exactly what outlines are for."

"Wait," said Clarke, squinting at Joseph's paper. "Your little brother is still standing there."

His brother pointed at the top of the page. "So why does your essay start at I if it's finished last?"

Joseph looked at the neat row of I, II, and III, then at the clock above the board, and grinned. "Because arguments go forward, even when we write them backward."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Most pencil cores are graphite powder mixed with clay, and adding more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks.
story:
Megan had one job in Mr. Karimi's art classroom: fill in the shading chart for her landscape project, from pale sky to dark hillside. The trouble started when she picked up two pencils that looked exactly the same size and found that one made a soft gray streak and the other barely left a ghost of a mark. She stared at the two lines on her paper. Same hand, same pressure, same paper. So what was different inside them?

"I need your pencils," she announced to Charlene, holding out her hand. "All of them." Charlene handed over three. Milania contributed two more, plus one she had borrowed from her grandfather's desk, and Megan lined them all up on the table like patients waiting for a checkup. Her grandfather had told her once, at his kitchen table, that most pencil cores are graphite powder mixed with clay. She hadn't thought much about it then, but now the question kept tickling her: if every core had the same stuff in it, what made the marks so different? Maybe it was the mixture itself.

She decided to test it. First she had to quantify how light each mark was, so she drew a small square with each pencil, held them in a row, and ranked them from palest to darkest. Milania pointed at the middle one. "That's the median," she said, tapping it. "Right in the center of the whole line." Then Megan pressed each pencil tip against her thumbnail, one by one. The palest ones felt firmer and barely dented; the darkest ones felt greasy and crumbly, and one even snapped when she leaned on it. She wrote her results in the corner of her sketchbook and frowned at the pattern. The harder the pencil, the lighter the mark. Every single time.

"So the clay," she said slowly, mostly to herself. "The clay must be doing it." If the core was graphite plus clay, and the pale pencils were the firm ones, then the ones with more clay were the hard ones, and the hard ones left the lighter marks. It fit every pencil on the table. It even fit the strange one from Milania's grandfather, which was hardest of all and almost invisible on the page. Megan grinned. She couldn't see inside a pencil, but she could still figure out what was hiding there.

For her sky she chose the hardest pencil, and for the hillside she chose the soft, dark one that Charlene warned her would smear if she sneezed on it. Mr. Karimi walked past, looked at the finished chart, and stopped. "That gradient is excellent. And I've been negligent, leaving the good pencils buried in that drawer all term." He slid the drawer open. Megan leaned over and pulled out a fat black pencil she had never tried. "Okay," she said, rolling it between her fingers, "what do you think this one is, mostly graphite or mostly clay?"

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: Rice seedlings are often grown first in a small nursery bed and then transplanted, often by hand, into flooded paddy fields.
story:
Nathaniel spread his notes across the library table and stared at the heading he had drafted the night before: HOW A MONSOON FORMS. Underneath it, so far, he had one sentence about wind and a doodle of a rain cloud wearing sunglasses. The presentation was Thursday, and today was Tuesday.

"You look like your project ate your homework," said Younes, sliding into the chair beside him.

"Worse. I have to explain why the monsoon matters for rice farming in South Asia, and I don't actually know why." Nathaniel tapped his pencil against the page. "The books say rice needs floods, and the monsoon brings floods, but that can't be the whole story. Somebody still has to get the rice into all that water."

Rosie arrived with an armload of books and dropped them onto the table with a thump that made a man at the next table glance over. "I found the farming ones," she said. "There's a whole shelf." She flipped one open to a photograph of workers bent over a flooded field, green stalks in their hands.

Nathaniel leaned in. The people weren't scattering seeds. They were pushing small plants into the mud, one at a time, row after row. He turned the page and found another picture, a crowded little bed of seedlings, thick as grass. He read the caption twice.

"The rice gets planted twice," he said slowly.

"Twice?" said Younes. "Why would anybody plant twice?"

"I don't know yet." Nathaniel copied the caption into his notes, word by word. First the seedlings grow in a small nursery bed. Then they get moved, often by hand, into the flooded paddy fields. "Wait," he said. "That means the farmers already know the floods are coming. They start the seedlings before the water arrives, then move them into the paddy when the monsoon fills it. The timing isn't luck. It's the whole point."

Rosie frowned. "But how do you prove that in a presentation? You can't exactly bring a paddy field to class."

"I can show the pattern," Nathaniel said. He grabbed a fresh sheet and drafted a timeline across the top: seedlings in the nursery, monsoon wind reversing, rain arriving, flooded fields, transplanting by hand. Then he tested it against the dates in the book, sliding each event along the line like beads on a string. If the seedlings started too late, the monsoon would come before they were ready, and the whole season would fail. If they started too early, the plants would grow tall and weak in the crowded nursery. Every date in the book fit.

Mr. Lin passed by their table on his rounds, wheeling the returns cart. "You three have been hovering over that paper like it's a treasure map."

"It kind of is," said Nathaniel. He showed Mr. Lin the timeline, tracing the arrows with his finger. "Land heats up, the wind reverses, moisture flows in from the ocean, and the rain floods the paddies. And the farmers time the seedlings to match."

Mr. Lin studied it and nodded. "Clear as a bell. But the picture of the seedlings is your strongest card. Lead with the surprise."

Thursday afternoon, Nathaniel stood at the front of the room and held up the photograph of the crowded nursery bed. "This is rice being planted the first time," he said. "Later, workers pull these seedlings up and move them, often by hand, into flooded paddy fields. That's the second planting." He watched Younes raise his hand and point at the timeline, and Rosie shoot him a vigorous thumbs-up from the third row.

"Want to see how a monsoon makes it all work?" Nathaniel asked the class, and picked up the marker.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Mandarin Chinese puts a measure word between a number and a noun: "one cat" is "yì zhī māo," where "zhī" is the measure word used for many animals.
story:
On Friday each student in Ms. Korhonen's Mandarin class had to stand up and describe their family and pets in full sentences, and Anthony had a problem: his grandmother's cat, the one he planned to talk about, was currently sleeping on the screen during their video call, blocking the only witness who could check his homework.

"Nǎinai," he said, "can you move Dumpling? I need to practice."

His grandmother nudged the cat aside and listened while he counted off on his fingers. "Wǒ yǒu yì māo," he said. "I have one cat."

"Yì zhī māo," she said gently, patting the air as if placing a small invisible word between his two.

Anthony wrote it down. At school the next day, Carl had drawn a flowchart on his binder to calibrate his sentence lengths, because Ms. Korhonen subtracted points for anything under three words. Simona, a veteran of two years of Mandarin classes, kept repeating her dog sentence under her breath like a spell. Anthony slid his notebook across the table.

"Why is there a zhī in mine?" he asked. "And look, yours has one too. Simona, say your dog sentence again."

She said it. Between the number and the dog sat the same little syllable, zhī, exactly where his grandmother had patted the air. Anthony went through the class handout with a pencil and found it again and again: number, then zhī, then the animal. Fish, cats, dogs, birds, all of them. His own sentence had left the middle out entirely, which meant he had been walking around saying something like "I have one, cat" all week. It was a vain hope that nobody had noticed.

He tested the pattern on Carl. "Say 'two cats,'" Anthony said, and when Carl produced the sentence with no middle word, Anthony held up his pencil like a fence between the number and the noun. "Something goes here. For animals it's zhī." Carl tried it, frowned, tried it again, and got it, and his face did the thing people's faces do when a pattern snaps into place.

There was one problem left. Did zhī work for a goldfish, and did it work for Dumpling's imaginary sworn enemy, the neighbor's pigeon, which his grandmother described in long, admiring sentences Anthony could not follow? He raised his hand and asked Ms. Korhonen only the first part, keeping the pigeon in reserve.

"In that case it's still zhī," she said, and moved on.

On Friday Anthony stood up, said he had one zhī cat and two zhī goldfish, and added, because he could not resist, "My grandmother has zero zhī pigeons, but the neighbor has very many."

Ms. Korhonen wrote something in her book. From two rows over, Simona mouthed the word many and grinned.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never.
story:
Ryan had downloaded the game because Tomas would not stop talking about it, and now he was sitting on Tomas's bedroom floor, phone in both hands, waiting for the next monster to appear on the map. A red shape blinked near the corner of the screen. "It's by the gas station," Tomas said, leaning over. "Go, go, it's a rare one."

But Ryan wasn't looking at the monster. He was looking at the little blue dot that marked where he was, and the faint circle around it, and the trail of tiny lines behind it. "Tomas," he said slowly. "Why does the game know we're at your house?"

"Because of the map, obviously." Tomas grabbed a chip.

"No, I mean it knows exactly. It knew when we walked to the kitchen. It knew when we went outside." Ryan had played for two days, and now that he thought about it, he could not remember the map ever being blank, not even when the game was closed and he was just checking the time. His impulsive side wanted to catch the red monster and forget it. Instead he pressed the home button and started digging through settings, trying to categorize what he found: screen time, notifications, privacy.

"It's not in the game's own settings," Evan said from the desk, where he was texting. Evan was the one at school who helped kids in the computer lab untangle their phones. "It's in the phone. Every app gets a choice, and you pick it yourself. Always, only while you're using it, or never."

Ryan found it. A list of every app, each one with a label beside it. His photos said Never. His music said While Using. The game, all the way at the bottom, said Always. He stared at the word. Always meant while he slept, while he was at school, while he carried the phone in his pocket to his grandmother's apartment across town. He pictured the trail of lines stretching out behind the little blue dot for two whole days, and somewhere, on some server, a copy of it sitting in a folder with his name on it.

Then a message popped up on the game's chat, from a player he had never met, with a username made of numbers. "Cool route yesterday," it said. "You take the park path at 4 most days?" Ryan's hands went cold. He read it twice. He had walked through the park yesterday at four, alone.

"Tomas. Look at this." He held out the phone. Tomas read it and stopped chewing.

Ryan went back into the settings, found the game's location line, and pressed it. Three choices sat there on the screen, exactly as Evan had said. He did not choose While Using. He pressed Never, and the little blue dot on the map winked out, and the trail of lines went with it. The red monster by the gas station was still blinking, but he closed the game anyway.

"Should we tell people at school?" Tomas asked.

Ryan was already typing the message to Evan. "Screenshot your game's settings," he wrote. "Check the bottom of the list."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Snapchat's Snap Map, launched in 2017, can show a user's real-time location to their friends on a map.
story:
Mya was lying on her bed with her phone two inches from her face when the group chat lit up. Tristen had typed, "Norah you're at the mall right now aren't you. In the game store." Mya sat up. She scrolled back through the messages. Nobody had said anything about the mall. Norah hadn't posted since lunch, when she'd written "brb." So how did Tristen know?

"how do u know that," Mya typed. Three dots appeared, then vanished, then appeared again. "lucky guess," Tristen answered, which felt ambiguous to Mya, like a note folded in half. A lucky guess could imply he really had guessed, or it could imply something else entirely. She chewed the end of her ponytail and decided to test it.

She messaged Tristen privately. "ok real answer or I'm asking Norah." A minute passed. Then Tristen sent a screenshot. It was a map of their town, tiny streets and the shape of the mall parking lot, with a little cartoon face floating over the game store. "it's called the Snap Map," he wrote. "it shows where people are, like, right now, if they're your friends on there." Mya stared at the little face. It had Norah's actual hairstyle drawn onto it.

Her first thought was that it was sort of amazing. Her second thought arrived slower, like a delayed text. The map hadn't known about Tristen's phone. It had known about Norah's. Which meant something on Norah's phone was telling a map where Norah was standing, all the time, and Norah hadn't even mentioned it. That was an inference, but a pretty solid one, because the little face had moved. Tristen sent a second screenshot a minute later and the face was now over the food court. Norah was apparently getting a pretzel.

Mya texted her directly. "do you know you're on the map thing?" The reply came fast: "WHAT map thing." Then: "wait. WAIT." Then a string of shocked face emojis. Mya called her, and Norah's voice came through breathless, pretzel crumbs audible. "Tristen knew I was in the game store? I never told anybody that." Norah had been planning to surprise Mya with a birthday gift, which was why she'd gone quiet after lunch, and now she was upset that the surprise had leaked out through her own pocket. "It's not your fault," Mya said. "You didn't know. I didn't know either until ten minutes ago."

Together, on the call, they hunted through the app until they found the settings, and Norah flipped her location to ghost mode with a tap. Tristen sent one more message to the group chat: "fair enough lol." Mya lay back down and looked at her phone differently now, like it was a window with the curtains open on her side too. She opened her own settings and found her little face sitting on her own street, patient and bright. She tapped it away, and the map went quiet and blank.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah, making the trip west far faster than by wagon.
story:
Chloe slid the microfilm reel into the reader and squinted at the blurry handwriting that filled the screen. Her history teacher, Ms. Zhang, had assigned the class a challenge: find one primary source, a diary or letter or newspaper from the time, and use it to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. Chloe wanted the best source in the room, and she had tracked down the 1866 diary of a woman named Harriet Poe, a settler who had crossed the plains with her family. The problem was that Harriet's handwriting slanted uphill, her spelling wandered, and half the pages looked like a storm had tried to demolish them.

"You're still on page four?" Rafaelle whispered from the next machine, where he was scrolling through an old land advertisement. "I've already got twelve reasons people went west. Gold, farmland, adventure."

"It's not a list contest," Chloe whispered back, though she privately wanted to win it anyway. She turned the crank slowly, and one entry sharpened into focus. May the ninth, it began. We have walked beside the wagon for thirty-one days. My shoes are gone and I have wrapped my feet in sacking. Lucca leaned over from across the table, read it, and pulled a face.

"Thirty-one days and they're not even there?" he said. "That's slower than my grandmother's internet." Chloe copied the line onto her notecard, and then she noticed something. Later entries in the diary stopped mentioning the wagon trail entirely, because the diary jumped ahead to 1869. Harriet's sister had written a letter, tucked between the pages, dated the tenth of May. "They joined the rails at Promontory Summit in Utah today," the letter said. "The railroad is finished from one coast to the other. Come home for Christmas, Harriet, and ride the train. You crossed in months. I could cross in days."

Chloe sat back. Months against days. She looked at her notecards, the one with the aching feet and the one with the letter, and tried out her idea on the others. "So here's my argument," she said, laying the cards in a row. "People moved west before the railroad because land and a fresh start were worth months of misery. Harriet proved that with her own feet. But the railroad changed the math. Once it was done, the trip west was far faster than by wagon, so the letter proves the second half." Rafaelle frowned at his twelve reasons. "That's actually coherent," he admitted. "Mine's just a pile of stuff."

When Ms. Zhang stopped at their table, Chloe pushed the diary pages across and said, "One settler, two dates, and a railroad." Ms. Zhang read the letter, then Harriet's wrapped feet, and raised her eyebrows at Chloe. "Ten May 1869," Chloe said, pointing at the date. "The day everything got faster." Ms. Zhang tapped the microfilm screen, right on the smudged ink where Harriet had written home that she had already bought her ticket.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is counted as a fallacy, a flaw in reasoning.
story:
Nicolas spread his note cards across the living room carpet like a general planning an invasion. His claim sat on the first card in thick black marker: School should start an hour later. The next three cards held evidence, quotes about sleep and grades that he had copied from a library book, and the last card was blank because he did not know what a warrant was supposed to be. Abbas sat on the couch eating crackers and reading the cards upside down.

"Ms. Ramos says the warrant is the part that connects the evidence to the claim," Nicolas said, tapping the empty card. "But what connects them? How does anyone know when it's there and when it isn't?"

Abbas shrugged and brushed cracker crumbs off the cushion. "Maybe it's like a bridge. You can't see a bridge working, you just notice when it's missing."

That idea followed Nicolas around all evening. He tested it on his own case. Evidence: students who sleep more get better grades. Claim: start school later. He asked himself, so what? Why did better grades follow from more sleep? He wrote, "because a rested brain learns better," and the empty card didn't look empty anymore. It was strange, he thought, how a missing piece could be invisible until you drew it in.

The real test came on Saturday, when Abbas and Nikola played the other side in a mock debate right there in the living room, Ms. Ramos volunteering as the judge from the armchair. Nicolas stood by the TV and delivered his first point, claim, evidence, warrant, all three parts clicking together. Then he argued that his opponents' study only surveyed twenty students. Nikola flushed and shot back, "You're just a sixth grader, what do you know about studies?"

Nicolas blinked. Something about the sentence felt off, the way a crooked picture frame feels off, though he couldn't say at first what was crooked about it. He watched Ms. Ramos's pen move across her scoring sheet, marking something down. When the round ended, she held up the sheet. "That comment cost you points," she told Nikola. "It's an ad hominem fallacy. It attacks the person making the claim instead of the claim itself."

Nikola groaned and sank low enough to submerge his face in the couch cushion. Nicolas, though, felt a spark of curiosity. He flipped a fresh card over and wrote: watch for attacks on the person, not the claim. A pattern, he realized, a rule you could carry into any argument, and no one could see the rule itself, only the places where it broke.

"Same time next Saturday?" Abbas asked, gathering the crackers.

"Bring harder arguments," Nicolas said, and stacked his cards into a neat block.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game; the Roman numeral 'Super Bowl I' was added later.
story:
Wyatt balanced a plate of chips on his knee and squeezed onto the end of the Ho family's couch. Mr. Ho had invited half the block over for the big game, and the living room was already loud, with Amber sprawled on the rug sketching the crowd of neighbors on her pad, because she wanted to fill her art notebook before the school show next week.

During a commercial, Mr. Ho's little cousin pointed at the screen and asked why the game had those weird letters after its name instead of a regular number. Nobody answered right away. Wyatt leaned forward and stared at the Roman numerals glowing behind the announcers. "Wait," he said. "Why do they use those? Nobody writes the World Series that way." Amber looked up from her drawing. "Maybe somebody just liked how it looked?" That didn't feel right to Wyatt. Style choices usually had a start somewhere, and he wanted to find it.

He borrowed Mr. Ho's phone from the counter and typed carefully, testing a hunch: if the numbering had been there from the beginning, some early article would show it. The results surprised him. "It wasn't called that at the start," he said. "The first one's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game." Amber set down her pencil. "Then when did the letters happen?" Wyatt scrolled, grinning. "The Roman numerals got added later. Like, they went back and called it Super Bowl I afterward." He read the line out loud twice so it would stick.

Mr. Ho came back from the kitchen with a tray of dumplings and raised an eyebrow. "You're telling me the first one had a different name entirely?" "Officially, yes," Wyatt said. "The Super Bowl I label came after." Mr. Ho chuckled and handed him a dumpling as payment for the fact. Amber frowned at her sketch, then flipped to the scoreboard in the corner of the page and lettered the game's number in Roman numerals with a fancy old-style border, as if it were an ancient artifact.

The game came back on, and the room groaned at a near interception. Wyatt noticed that the crowd's roar seemed to coincide exactly with the moment the flag appeared, so the officials must have been deciding while everyone was still reacting. "Referees have a rough job," Amber's dad said from the armchair. "Everybody wants them to be impartial, but every single fan in this room is sure they're wrong." Amber snorted without looking up from her drawing.

Wyatt found himself watching the announcers more than the plays now. If the name had been changed once, he wondered, what else on the broadcast had been patched and relabeled over the years? He noticed how the old highlight clips in a montage had a grainy, washed-out look compared with the live picture, like erosion on a riverbank, the image wearing down a little every time it was copied and recopied. "Look at the old footage," he said, pointing. "It's literally dissolving." Amber added tiny speckles to the corner of her scoreboard to match.

At the two-minute warning, Amber turned her notebook around so everyone could see the finished page: the whole living room crammed onto the couch, the dumpling tray, and the game's Roman numerals lettered in gold. Mr. Ho held it up beside the television. "That belongs in a frame," he said. Wyatt copied the championship game's original name onto a napkin and folded it into his pocket, in case anyone ever asked him the question again.

The kicker lined up for a field goal, and the whole room stood at once. "If we win this," Amber whispered, "I'm drawing the pile-on." The ball sailed through the uprights, and Mr. Ho's cousin threw popcorn at the ceiling fan.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Repeating an experiment several times helps show whether a result is real or just happened by chance.
story:
Jayden had exactly forty minutes before the science fair judges reached his table, and his bean plants were refusing to cooperate. He had planted ten cups, five with music played over them for a week and five in silence, because his hypothesis said music would make them grow taller. Now the silent cups held leafy green stems while the music cups sat short and sad, like they had been to a concert they hated.

"That's not fair," said Elaine, leaning over his table. "One of my volcano entries fizzled last year. Twice." She pointed at his cups. "Those imply your idea was wrong. Or maybe your speakers were terrible."

"They were my dad's old headphones," Jayden admitted. Behind them, a kid named after nobody in particular was yelling across the gymnasium, because his toy car had just won one race down a ramp and he was now announcing to everyone that it was the fastest car forever, that no car would ever beat it.

"That was one race," Rita said to him, arms crossed. "My car could win the next one."

"Impossible," the kid said. "Mine is the fastest forever."

Jayden watched the second race. Rita's car won by half a car length. The kid's face went through several stages of grief in about four seconds. Then he demanded a third race, and a fourth, and by the fifth race everyone could see the truth: the two cars traded wins almost evenly. One race had meant nothing.

Jayden stared at his own table. One week of music, one result. But his watering schedule had been sparse on Tuesday and Thursday because he had soccer practice, and the music cups happened to sit closest to the window, where the sun baked them every afternoon. Maybe his experiment hadn't really tested music at all. Maybe it had tested heat and forgetfulness.

"We could run it again," Rita said, following his gaze. "Right here. You have the cups, you have the headphones."

"Judges in twenty minutes," Elaine said, tapping the clock on the wall.

They pivoted fast. Jayden moved the cups away from the window, watered everything evenly, and played music to a fresh set of five cups Rita had brought as spares, timing nothing, just watching. While the music played, they ran the results again with the old cups, swapping positions so the sunny side went to the silent group this time. Ten minutes later the tall cups were the tall cups no matter where they sat, and the short ones stayed short. Twice tested, same answer.

When Ms. Farah stopped at his table with her clipboard, Jayden pointed at the two neat rows. "My hypothesis said music helps plants. I tested it twice, and twice the music plants lost." He grinned. "So I was wrong, and I can prove it."

Ms. Farah wrote something down and smiled. "That," she said, "is the best sentence I've heard all day."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Brackets are cleared with the distributive property before solving: 3(x + 2) becomes 3x + 6, because the 3 multiplies both terms inside.
story:
Cooper slid his math notebook across the kitchen table until it bumped Asiya's elbow. "Mr. Hamdan says the quiz is tomorrow, and I still don't get the ones with brackets."

Asiya tapped the page with her pencil. "Like that one. 3(x + 2) = 15. Aviana did it last night and got the wrong answer, and she won't believe me when I say why."

From the counter, where she was negotiating with Cooper's dad for an extra cookie, Aviana called over, "I did not get it wrong. The book is wrong."

They pulled her over to the table anyway. Aviana flopped into the third chair, still holding her cookie, and wrote out her work in loopy purple pen: 3(x + 2) = 15, then 3x + 2 = 15. She subtracted 2 from both sides, divided both sides by 3, and announced, "x equals thirteen thirds."

"That's not even a whole number," Cooper said. The kitchen smelled like burnt toast from the cookie batch, and the overhead light buzzed a little. "Mr. Hamdan said we should always check by putting the answer back in. Try it."

Aviana substituted thirteen thirds for x. Her numbers got uglier and uglier, and her spine curved lower over the table as she worked, until her braids nearly touched the paper. "That's not fifteen," she admitted. "That's nowhere near fifteen."

Cooper stared at her first step. Something about it looked off, the way a picture looks off when one corner hangs lower than the other. He grabbed a fresh sheet and wrote 3(x + 2) twice. "You multiplied only the x," he said slowly. "But the 3 is outside the brackets, so it has to hit both things inside." He wrote underneath: 3x + 6 = 15. Then he subtracted 6 from both sides, because whatever you did to one side you had to do to the other, and divided. "x equals three."

"Check it," Asiya said, mouth full of cookie crumbs.

Cooper put 3 back in. 3(3 + 2) was 3 times 5, which was 15. The equation balanced, like a seesaw level and still.

Aviana crossed out her purple work with one long dramatic line. "Fine. FINE." She copied Cooper's first step into her own notebook, then did the next problem, 4(x + 1) = 20, without stopping. "Four x plus four," she muttered. "Equals twenty. Subtract four from both sides. Divide. Three." She looked up, startled. "It checks."

Cooper grinned and flipped to the next problem in the book, one with a 2 outside the brackets and a minus sign inside. His pencil made a soft scratching sound on the paper. "This one's mine."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: In the Scripps National Spelling Bee, a speller may start over, but changing any letters already said counts as a misspelling.
story:
The community center gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn, and Declan was on the stage with his hands sweating through his number card, number 14. He had wanted this since third grade, when he'd spelled "catastrophe" wrong in front of the whole cafeteria and had to sit down while Darren made a tiny violin motion at him from the lunch line. Today Darren and Finlay sat in the second row, and Mr. Yoon, who ran the center's Tuesday study hall, was the pronouncer, wearing a tie with the alphabet on it.

"Catastrophe," Mr. Yoon said, and Declan almost laughed. The universe had a sense of humor, apparently.

"Catastrophe. C-A-T..." He got to the S and his brain did the thing brains do, the thing where it holds up two doors and both say S behind them. Was it an S with a PH after, or was there an F somewhere? "A-S-T-R-O..." He stopped. The gym went so quiet he could hear the popcorn machine in the hallway, ticking like it was counting down the suspense for him.

Here was the problem. He had already said R-O, and somewhere in the back of his mind he remembered reading the rules on the drive over, mainly to postpone thinking about the word "turbulent," which was apparently in the study list. The rule had said a speller could start over. But you could not change any letters you had already said, because that counted as a misspelling. So if he restarted and swapped an S for an F, he was out, and Darren would do the violin thing again, but slower this time, for drama.

Declan said, "May I start over, please?"

"You may," said Mr. Yoon.

So the only safe plan was to say the exact same letters again and figure out the ending before he ran out of road. "C-A-T-A-S-T-R-O." He glanced at Finlay, who was mouthing something that was either "ph" or "help." Darren was holding up a pretend umbrella, which meant nothing, except that Darren thought it meant something.

"P-H-E," Declan said.

"Correct."

Finlay stood up and sat back down immediately, like his body had acted without permission. On the next round, a kid named number 9 started "turbulent," got to the second T, and asked to start over. Declan leaned forward, curious whether the kid knew the rule. He restarted, and out loud, in front of everyone, changed his second T to an N. The bell dinged before he'd even finished breathing.

"Changing a letter after you've said it counts as a misspelling," Mr. Yoon said gently, and number 9 walked off shaking his head at his own shoes.

Declan stopped feeling smug about halfway to feeling smug, because he realized he'd nearly done the same thing five minutes ago. He'd only escaped because of a rule he'd read to avoid worrying. In the final round, down to him and one other kid, Mr. Yoon said, "Perseverance."

"P-E-R-S-E-V," Declan began, then heard himself say, "E-R-A-N-C-E," and felt the floor tilt. He'd left out the second E. He asked to start over, said the same letters again, and the word came out right the second time, all of it, E and all.

Afterward Darren found him by the popcorn machine. "I was signaling the umbrella," he said. "You know. Ph sounds like F. Weather. Turbulent skies."

"That is the worst code ever invented," said Declan, holding his trophy.

"Worked, didn't it?" said Darren, and stole a handful of popcorn.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The cell wall is the thick outer border you see around each onion cell, making the cells look like rows of bricks.
story:
The community garden had one shed nobody used, and today Mr. Nasser unlocked it and carried out a microscope. "Gardening club meets science club," he announced, and his grin was infectious. Jackson was first in line.

"Every gardener should know what they're actually growing," Mr. Nasser said, handing out onions from the storage bin. "Peel the thinnest skin layer you can from the inside of an onion, lay it flat on a slide, one drop of water, and a cover slip." He showed them once and then stepped back, arms crossed, like he was daring them to figure the rest out themselves.

Jackson peeled carefully, but his skin folded and the edge tore. When he looked through the eyepiece, he saw a blurry smear of grey. Miko, on his left, gasped at her own slide. "Oh wow. I think I grew a brick wall." She yanked Jackson over. "Look. Rows of bricks, like a little garden wall."

Jackson pressed his eye to her lens. She was right: neat rectangles stacked in lines, each outlined by a thick dark border. She was already flipping through the class worksheet. "The paper says label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus." She frowned. "But I don't have cells, I have a brick wall. My slide must be wrong."

"It's not wrong," Jackson said slowly. He looked again, moving the slide a hair to the left. Every single rectangle had a faint line just inside the border, and in some of them a dark dot sat near the middle. His heart started thumping. "Miko. Each brick is a single cell." He pointed at the thick outer edge. "That's the cell wall. The fainter line inside it is the membrane. And those dots are nuclei."

Miko stared at the slide, then at him, then back. "So I'm looking at thousands of onion cells at once." She grabbed the worksheet and started labelling so fast her pencil squeaked. Marc-Olivier crowded in from the right. "My smear is just grey, what's the secret?"

"Thinner skin," Jackson said, already hunting through the onion for a fresh layer. "And flat, not folded." He peeled again, slower this time, breathing like the coach taught him before a race. The new skin was almost invisible, like a bubble of glass. He lowered the cover slip and bent to the eyepiece.

There they were: rows of bricks, wall, membrane, dot. He drew them all, then checked his sketch against the diagrams in the garden club's old database of plant records, and his hand shot up so fast it nearly knocked the slide off the stage. "Mr. Nasser! Mine works! Come interpret this!"

Mr. Nasser leaned in, looked for a long moment, and said, "Textbook."

"Better than the textbook," Jackson said. "I grew it myself."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A null hypothesis is the statement that there is no relationship between the things being studied, which an experiment then tries to reject.
story:
Sofia dragged the seed trays onto Mr. Sultani's workbench before he had even finished unlocking the garage. "We get the whole workshop today?" Peter asked, spinning a stool. "For science," Sofia said, patting the two bags of potting soil like they were treasure. She and Peter and Daisy had one week to test their idea for the school fair: music makes plants grow faster. Mr. Sultani had offered the garage because it stayed warm, and he promised not to peek.

"First we write down our guess," Daisy said, flipping open the notebook. "Our hypothesis." Sofia nodded, but then she frowned at the blank page. A question kept sneaking up on her, and she couldn't evade it the way she had in class, where she could just wait for someone else to answer. "Okay, but what if music does nothing at all?" she asked. "What does that look like?" Peter shrugged. "Then both groups of seedlings are the same height, I guess." Daisy's pen stopped. "So we have to say that first. That's what a null hypothesis is, the statement that there's no relationship between the things you're studying." She wrote it out: no relationship between music and growth. "Then we try to knock it down."

Sofia remembered the exact moment the whole project had started, three weeks ago, when the anonymous note appeared in her locker. Someone had slipped her a folded page that said only, "My mom talks to her ferns and they're huge." No name, no signature. It had plagued her all afternoon, that mystery, until she decided the only way to answer it was with an experiment. Talking, singing, it was all sound. Sound was testable.

They planted forty seeds, twenty in each tray, and set Tray A on the shelf beside the old radio Daisy had brought from home. Tray B went on the opposite bench, behind the cardboard wall Peter built so it couldn't even hear a whisper of the music. Every morning they would measure, and every afternoon the radio would play for an hour while Tray B sat in silence. "If the null hypothesis survives," Sofia said, hammering a label onto each tray, "we have to say music doesn't help. Even if we hate it."

Mr. Sultani leaned in the doorway with two mugs of cocoa. "Six days until the fair," he said. "You nervous?" "No," said Sofia. Then she grinned. "Okay, yes. But mostly I want Friday to come." Daisy clicked the radio on, and music crackled out over Tray A while Sofia crouched with the ruler, waiting for the first green tip to break the soil. "Grow, little guys," she whispered. "Prove us right."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The Panic of 1837 caused a long economic depression in the United States, and many ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land.
story:
Liam had a history essay due Monday and nothing to write it with. The assignment said to use a primary source, something written by an actual person at the time, to explain why families moved west in the 1800s. His textbook gave one paragraph of vague reasons, so on Saturday his mother drove him to Grandpa's house, where the attic held four boxes of old family papers.

The attic smelled like dust and cedar. Liam's grandfather pointed at a shoebox tied with shoelace. "That came from your great-great-great-grandmother. Careful with it." Liam untied the lace and found a diary with a cracked leather cover, its pages brown at the edges. He sat cross-legged under the single bulb and turned the pages one at a time, reading the slanted handwriting.

October 1837: "The bank has taken the farm. Father says we are ruined." A later entry: "We will go to the frontier. Land there is cheap and the soil is black and deep." Liam read the lines twice. Ruined. He had seen that word in a movie about card games, but it did not fit here. He carried the diary downstairs, where his grandfather was slicing an apple.

"Grandpa, what happened to farms in 1837?" Liam asked. "Was it just our family?" His grandfather shook his head. "They called it the Panic of 1837. After that came hard times for years, and a lot of ruined farmers packed up and headed west for cheap, fertile land." Liam wrote the phrase in his notebook. So the diary line was not just one family's bad luck. It was a piece of something bigger, and the something bigger explained why anyone would load a wagon and take a dangerous trail across the country. He tested the idea against the next entries: sold the oxen, bought a second ox, a cousin in Ohio also leaving. The pattern held.

On Sunday Liam drafted the essay at his kitchen table. He put the diary line first and let it carry the argument. He underlined the date, because Ms. Rodríguez always said to emphasize the evidence that mattered most. In his conclusion he wrote that a family like his would only risk disease, river crossings, and a whole season of walking if staying meant losing everything. The diary's last page in the box was from 1844, written in a different hand: "We have our land. The children are resilient after all that walking, and the corn is in."

Monday morning, Ms. Rodríguez read the essay during silent work, then set it on Liam's desk with a sticky note on top. He peeled it off and read her handwriting: "This is exactly what a primary source is for." He turned around in his seat and held the note up so Charles, two rows back, could see it. "Read this," Liam said.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: In Buddhism, reaching nirvana ends the cycle of rebirth by ending the craving and ignorance that keep it going.
story:
Raphael spread his poster board across the kitchen table, moving the salt shaker and a bowl of washwater out of the way. The assignment from Ms. Nkosi was due first period tomorrow: a chart comparing how two faiths explain what happens after death. His mother stood at the counter rinsing a package of pork intestines for tomorrow's soup, and the smell of vinegar filled the room.

Norman had come over to work on his own chart, but he kept checking the clock above the stove. "I need to leave by seven for Diego's game," he said. "Can we do the easy parts first?"

"There are no easy parts," Raphael said. He had drawn two columns, Christianity and Buddhism, and under Christianity he had written clearly: after death the soul goes to heaven or hell, and that is the end of the road. Under Buddhism he had written: people are reborn again and again. Then he had stopped, because the third row of the chart asked how the cycle ends, and his hand was hovering over the marker with nothing to write.

"Write that it never ends," Norman said. "Reincarnation just keeps going forever. That's what my cousin said."

Raphael tapped the marker against his teeth. If the cycle never ended, then the third row would be blank, and Ms. Nkosi never left blank rows on her charts on purpose. A blank row felt like a clue that he was wrong. He decided to test Norman's answer the only way he could without leaving the kitchen: the dictionary, the encyclopedia volume on the shelf by the fridge, and Ms. Nkosi herself, who lived next door and was watering her plants on her porch.

He went out the back door and asked her straight out, "Does the rebirth cycle in Buddhism ever stop?"

She set down the watering can. "Read me your third row when you find out," she said, and handed him a thin book from her windowsill. "Look up nirvana."

Back inside, he found the entry while his mother dropped the intestines into the pot with a hiss. The words were plain: reaching nirvana ends the cycle of rebirth by ending the craving and ignorance that keep it going. Raphael read it twice, then wrote it into the row, word by word, so it matched the book exactly.

"You wasted ten minutes," Norman said, but he leaned over to read it. "Wait. So the cycle has a stop button. Craving and ignorance. That's not trivial, that's the whole answer." He copied the line onto his own chart in his fastest handwriting, then closed his notebook and grabbed his jacket.

The twist came when Raphael flipped back to his first row. His note under Buddhism said people are reborn "because they want things," which was only half of it, and now he could fix it. He crossed out his sentence and added ignorance beside craving. Norman pounded on the door frame from the porch.

"Tell Diego I'm coming!" he shouted, and his sneakers slapped down the steps.

Raphael capped the marker and looked at the chart. In the pot on the stove, the water had begun to boil.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
story:
Grayson set his phone face-down next to his plate, then turned it over again, because the photo Miles had sent him at three o'clock was still bothering him. It showed Philippe's new bike leaning against a garage, and underneath it Miles had written only "so jealous." Grayson's mom scooped rice onto his plate and asked how his day was, and he said fine, but his thumb was already tapping the info button beside the picture.

There it was. Not the bike, not the garage. A small map, and on the map a pin, and the pin sat on Willow Crescent, which was Miles's own street. Grayson had never tapped that button before in his life. The screen showed numbers too, coordinates that looked like nonsense until he pasted them into a map app and watched the view pivot from the whole country down to one gray roof he recognized from riding past it every weekend. His mom asked if he was going to eat or just stare, and he picked up his fork.

"Your phone writes where the photo was taken into the file," he said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "Hidden data. It's called EXIF metadata." He had found those words on the screen itself, small and opaque under a heading he'd had to squint at. "Miles didn't type his address anywhere. It just... came with the bike."

His mom leaned over. "You can see that?"

"Anybody can see that, if they know where to look." He articulated the next part carefully, because saying it made it more real than thinking it. "Miles posted that photo to the group chat. That's twelve people. And the coach's assistant. And whoever else anybody forwarded it to."

He was about to text Miles a warning when his own phone buzzed. A comment, on a photo Grayson himself had posted last week, of the lasagna his mom had made. He had taken it right at this table. The account commenting had no picture, no name he knew, just a string of letters and numbers. The comment said: "Nice dinner. Blue door, right? Corner house?"

Grayson's fork stopped halfway to his mouth. Slowly, without a word, he tapped the info button on his own lasagna photo, the button he had not known existed until tonight. The map unfolded. The pin dropped. It stood exactly where he was sitting, above the kitchen, above the blue door on the corner house, above the plate of food going cold in front of him.

He turned the phone toward his mom so she could see the pin, and then looked at the window, where the curtain hung open and the streetlight made a long bright stripe across the table.

"Lock the door," he said.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A baking soda volcano erupts because baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) reacts with vinegar (acetic acid) to produce carbon dioxide gas.
story:
Mia had built her volcano twice already, and both times it had barely fizzled. Now she stood at the back counter of the science classroom, third volcano in front of her, remembering how she had chosen this project in the first place. Last year she had copied a kit straight from the box, and Ms. Wardak had written "Where is the question?" in red pen across the top of her worksheet. This year there would be a question. Her question was: what actually makes the eruption happen, since nobody could see it?

"It's the gas," Graeme said, tipping baking soda into the crater. "Baking soda, or sodium bicarbonate, reacts with vinegar, acetic acid, and you get carbon dioxide gas. That's the whole push." He said it the way he said everything, like he had read it somewhere and was daring the world to prove it wrong.

"Then more vinegar should mean more gas," Mia said. She had set out four cups on the counter, each with a different amount of vinegar, and a ruler taped to the wall behind the volcano to measure how high the foam climbed. Graeme wanted more than a plain volcano anyway; he wanted a graph. She poured the smallest cup first. The foam rose two centimeters. The next cup, twice as much, sent it nearly to the top of the ruler. She wrote both numbers down, feeling like she was finally doing something instead of just watching something.

Hannah leaned over the tray of paper cups they were using as molds. "Careful, the dried ones get brittle if you leave them overnight," she said, nudging a cracked cup out of the way so it wouldn't obstruct the view of the eruption zone. Mia poured the third cup, the biggest one, and waited for the fountain.

Nothing like it. The foam bulged, sputtered, and dribbled down the side, lower than the second trial. Mia stared at it. The gas had to be there, the same as before, so why had the eruption shrunk? She looked at the crater, then at the cardboard tube inside it, and realized the opening was packed solid with wet baking soda from the earlier trials. She dug it clear with a spoon, ran the same amount of vinegar again, and this time the foam shot past the ruler entirely and splattered Hannah's sleeve. Ms. Wardak looked up from her desk. "Someone will be explaining that graph to the judges on Friday," she said. Graeme was already drawing a second column on the data sheet. "Trial five," he said, holding out the cup.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: PolitiFact, a US fact-checking website founded in 2007, rates claims on a scale it calls the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire.
story:
Joseph was telling everyone on the bus that the city was going to tear down the roller rink and put in a parking garage, and he was enjoying the attention way too much. "My cousin heard it from a guy who works for the city," he said, leaning into the aisle so the kids three rows back could hear. "They already signed the papers."

Justin gripped his backpack strap. The rink was where he and Joseph and Lola had spent every Friday since sixth grade, and last spring he had bailed on Lola's birthday party there because Joseph said the buses on Fridays were "unsafe," which had turned out to mean one kid got sick once. He still felt bad about that. Now he squinted at Joseph and said, "Which guy? What's his name?"

Joseph shrugged. "Does it matter?"

"It matters if it's true," Lola said from the seat behind them. She smelled like the cherry lip balm she put on when she was thinking hard, and she was clicking the cap on and off. "My mom says people say stuff on the bus all day and nobody checks any of it."

"That's an opinion," Joseph said. "I'm allowed to have opinions."

"You said they signed papers," Justin said slowly, working it out. "That's not an opinion. An opinion is like, the rink smells like feet. You can't check that. Papers either exist or they don't." He could see Joseph's jaw tighten, the way it did when a debate started slipping away from him. Joseph wanted to be the kid with the inside story, the one people leaned toward on the bus, and for a second Justin almost let it go.

Instead he pulled out his phone. "My dad and I looked something up last month," he said, "a claim in a TV ad. PolitiFact. It's a fact-checking website, founded in 2007, and it rates claims on a scale called the Truth-O-Meter." Lola leaned over the seat, close enough that he could feel the cold air coming off the window near her sleeve. "It goes from True all the way to Pants on Fire," Justin said. "That's the worst one."

They typed in the rink. The first result was a story from two weeks ago: the city council had voted to keep the rink and renovate it, money already approved. No garage, no papers, nothing signed. Joseph went quiet, watching the phone like it might change its answer.

"It's ironic," Lola said finally, capping her lip balm. "The rink stays open, and the only thing that got torn down was your story." She stood up as the bus lurched toward their stop, one hand on the cold metal rail, and looked back at Joseph. "Friday. Seven o'clock. Bring your skates, and your Truth-O-Meter."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the United States, the cost of crude oil is usually the largest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so pump prices tend to rise when crude oil prices rise.
story:
The last pint of strawberries at Ms. Haile's stall had a hand-lettered sign taped to it, and the price had been crossed out and rewritten twice. Lillian stared at the new number. Last week the same berries had cost half as much, and there had been a whole flat of them, red and gleaming, with nobody fighting over the last few. She had spent her money on honey instead, telling herself the berries would still be there tomorrow. Now three people stood in line behind her, and Ms. Haile's forehead had begun to perspire as she counted change fast.

"They were four dollars all June," Lillian said, holding up the pint. "Why eight now?"

"Frost took half the crop up the valley," Ms. Haile said. "Everybody who wants berries this week wants these." She tapped the sign. "Scarce and wanted means dear. Plentiful means cheap. Ask the zucchini people." Behind her, a farmer was practically giving away squash, calling out two for a dollar to anyone who glanced his way.

Jade elbowed up beside Lillian with her dad, who was parking the car at the gas station across the lot. A boy at the pump was tugging his mother's sleeve and pointing at the sign there. "Mom, why is it more than last week?" His mother shrugged, but Jade's dad answered over his shoulder without looking up from the nozzle. "Crude oil got expensive. Crude oil is usually the biggest single part of the price of a gallon of gas, so when crude goes up, pump prices tend to go up too." The boy nodded like he'd been handed the answer to a riddle, and Jade's dad smiled, almost ironic, since he was filling the tank anyway.

Lillian turned the idea over like a lens in her hand, tilting it to see whether it was true. She walked the row of stalls like a scientist, testing. The peach stand had one basket left and a crowd, and the price was high. The lettuce table had crates and crates and a bored farmer, and the price was so low a woman bought four heads. Same rule, two ways. She thought about last Saturday, the honey, the berries she had assumed would wait for her, and she couldn't decide whether she had been patient or just foolish. Maybe both.

She counted her money on the bench near the fountain. Eight dollars exactly, the whole of it, which meant no honey, no peach cider, nothing else all morning. She looked at the pint in her hand, then at the lettuce stand, where four heads would cost two dollars and feed her family a week. The line behind her lengthened. Jade waved from across the lot. Lillian took a breath, pushed through the crowd, and set the strawberries back on Ms. Haile's scale. "Two heads of lettuce," she said, "and the biggest one you've got."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: If Earth's axis had no tilt, sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year, so there would be almost no seasons.
story:
Aiden had a globe, a desk lamp, and one night to figure out the seasons before Mr. Suryanto's science class made their presentations in the morning. The assignment said each student had to explain, with a model, why summer and winter happen. He had tried reading the chapter twice, and both times the words slid off without sticking.

Maelly came over after dinner with a bag of popcorn and her notebook. "My mom had to authorize the sleepover swap, so I can stay till nine," she said, dropping onto the rug beside him. "Show me what you've got."

Aiden plugged in the lamp and set the globe on the floor a step away. "Mr. Suryanto said to use the lamp as the sun," he said. He spun the globe slowly. "So Earth goes around like this, and it turns, and then... seasons." He stopped. He realized he had no idea what came next.

"That's your whole presentation?" Maelly pulled a kernel from the bag. "Mariah brought in a contemporary one off the internet for extra credit, with diagrams. She'll do a whole critique of yours if you just say 'and then seasons.'"

Aiden tilted the globe so its stand held it leaning, the way it sat in the classroom. Then he walked it in a slow circle around the lamp, keeping the lean pointed at the same wall the whole time. At one side of the circle, the top half of the globe caught the light straight on while the bottom half sat in shadow. At the other side, it flipped.

"Look at Canada," he said. "It's lit up like noon. Australia's in the dark." He kept walking the circle. "Now Canada's dark and Australia's bright. Same globe, same lamp. It's the lean."

Maelly leaned in. "So try it without the lean."

That was the part neither of them expected. Aiden held the globe perfectly upright in his fist, no tilt at all, and walked it around the lamp again. Canada caught the light at exactly the same angle on every lap. Australia did too. Every place on the globe got its same slant of light all the way around, lap after lap, and the bright patch never moved north or south. The seasons had simply gone.

"If Earth's axis had no tilt," Aiden said slowly, watching the unchanging light, "sunlight would hit each place at the same angle all year." He set the globe down on its tilted stand and did one more lap, watching the light climb and fall. "There'd almost be no seasons at all. It would just be the same weather forever."

At nine, Maelly called her mom from the kitchen. Aiden stood the lamp on his desk where he could see it from bed and walked the globe around it one more time, keeping the lean pointed at the closet door.

"No seasons," he said to the upright globe in his other hand. "Not a single one."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Like humans, guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C, so they must get it from their food every day.
story:
Sydney carried the cardboard carrier through Riverside Park like it held something breakable, which it did. Inside, curled on a towel, was Peanut, her brand-new guinea pig, won after two weeks of arguing her case at the dinner table. Her dad had said pets were a big responsibility. Sydney had said she knew. Now, walking past the duck pond, she wasn't so sure she knew anything at all, because Peanut had barely touched his food this morning.

At the picnic tables by the playground, Tori and Vayda were waiting with the sunflower seeds they always brought. Tori was a veteran pet owner, with two rabbits and a hamster behind her, and she leaned over the carrier immediately. "He's got that hunched-up look," she said. "My rabbit did that when he was sick."

Sydney's stomach dropped. She tried to think backward through the last three days, the way her mom untangled problems at work. She had fed Peanut exactly what the pet store sold her, a bowl of dry pellets, morning and night. She had refilled his water. She had cleaned the cage. Nothing fresh, though. Not one piece of vegetable, because she'd been afraid of giving him something wrong. She remembered the binder from the school library, the one she'd flipped through on the bus during her long commute across town, and one page swam back to her. "Wait," she said slowly. "Guinea pigs can't make their own vitamin C. They have to get it from their food every single day. And I haven't given him anything with vitamin C in it. Pellets alone might not be enough."

"So it's like he got sick from missing breakfast, basically," Vayda said. "Gross breakfast, but still."

It was a guess, but it was a testable one. Sydney dug through the backpack she'd packed like a first-aid kit, just in case: a red bell pepper, bought that morning from the corner store with her allowance. She set a strip of it in the carrier and the three of them crouched on the grass in the shade of an oak, watching, saying nothing, while a jogger thumped past on the gravel path. Peanut's nose twitched. Then he was chewing, fast and greedy, whiskers trembling.

"Okay," Tori whispered, like loud voices might scare the appetite away. "Okay, that's a good sign."

Sydney didn't celebrate yet. She knew one pepper strip wasn't a cure, and she knew that in a few days, if her guess was right, Peanut would perk up, and if it was wrong, she'd be on the phone with a vet. It had been a little vain of her, she thought, to assume the pet store bag held everything a living thing needed, just because it had a picture of a guinea pig on the front. She made a note in her phone: pepper or greens, every day, no exceptions.

Peanut finished the strip and made a sound Sydney had never heard before, a squeaky little wheek aimed straight at her.

"That means he likes you," Tori said. "Or he's begging for more."

"Both," said Sydney, and she opened the backpack again.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.
story:
The vase was already broken when Jaxon got to the kitchen, which was the only fact nobody argued about. Emilee stood over the shards with a dustpan, and Nevaeh was on her knees trying to glue two pieces together with a glue stick, which was not going to work.

"My grandma's coming at five," Emilee said. "She gave us that vase. We have maybe forty minutes to figure out what happened so we can tell her something."

"That's not much time," Jaxon said.

So they interviewed the household. Emilee's dad said the cat did it, absolutely, the cat had it coming to him for months. Her little brother said Emilee had bumped the table doing a dance move. Emilee said she'd been upstairs the whole time and the brother was blaming her because he'd been dribbling a basketball indoors. Even the grandmother, reached by phone, said the vase had been sitting too close to the edge for weeks, which was practically nobody's fault.

Jaxon wrote all four stories in his notebook and stared at them. Same broken vase, four versions, none of them matching. Something about it tickled the back of his brain, and then he had it.

"My cousin made me watch this old movie," he said. "Rashomon. Akira Kurosawa, 1950. It tells one crime through four witnesses, and every account contradicts the others. Nobody even agrees on what happened."

"So the movie is about this?" Neavaeh said, gesturing at the shards with the glue stick.

"It's about people," Emilee said, in the tone of someone who had consumed an entire documentary series on human nature over spring break. "Everybody sees the thing that makes them feel okay."

Jaxon tested it. He checked the table, which was a solid wooden plateau in the middle of the kitchen, flat and level, no wobble. He checked the shards: the break pattern came from the side facing the hallway, not the stairs, not the living room where the cat slept. A basketball bouncing was probable; a cat leaping four feet sideways onto a heavy vase was not. The brother's story matched the physics, which meant the brother had done it and had still told a lie inside the truth.

"There were two people who could have done it," Jaxon said. "And four stories. That's the weird part."

"Grandma's pulling into the driveway," Emilee said, dropping the dustpan. "Nevaeh, sweep. Jaxon, notebook away. Everybody, casual."

The door opened, and the grandmother walked in carrying flowers for the empty spot.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Specific details, like 'Grandma's red bicycle' instead of 'a bike', give an improv partner more to build on.
story:
Maelie stood at the edge of the drama camp stage with her sneakers glued to the floor, which was a problem, because in improv you were supposed to move. The gym smelled like floor wax and old costumes, and somewhere behind her Jaxton was already bouncing on his toes like this was the easiest thing in the world.

"Two of you up," said Mr. Jean-Louis, clapping his hands. "Scene is a garage. Go."

Jaxton launched in. "Hey, look at all this stuff."

"Yeah," Maelie said. "Lots of stuff."

They shuffled around an imaginary garage for a minute, picking up nothing, describing nothing. Jaxton said, "This is interesting." Maelie said, "Sure is." Eventually they ran out of ways to say nothing, and they just stood there while the rest of the campers shifted on the bleachers. Mr. Jean-Louis called time and made a small note on his clipboard. Maelie's ears went hot.

At lunch she sat with Ezekiel, who had been in the morning group and whose scene had actually worked. "What did you do?" she asked, tearing her sandwich into smaller and smaller pieces without eating any of it.

"I said I found a note in my mom's coat pocket," Ezekiel said. "Then my partner had a note to react to. A real one, in her head." He shrugged and stole one of her pickle slices. "You two were just handing each other fog."

Maelie pushed her tray aside and thought about that. Fog. When Jaxton said stuff, she had nowhere to put her hands, nothing to picture, no reason to care. But a note in a coat pocket, that was a thing you could hold. She turned it over the way she turned over the vending machine trick at school, the one where a slow second button press sometimes freed the stuck chips. One test. That was all she needed.

Back in the gym, Mr. Jean-Louis paired them again. Same scene, a garage. Maelie's stomach did a slow flip, but she stepped onto the taped square first this time.

"Careful," she said, lifting a paint can that wasn't there. "Don't knock over Grandma's red bicycle."

Jaxton blinked, and then his whole face changed. He grabbed imaginary handlebars. "This thing? Grandma raced this. She won a trophy on it in 1972, and now it's mine."

"No way," Maelie said. "You promised we'd fix it together. You said we'd ride it to the lake."

"I said no such thing." Jaxton swung a leg over the invisible frame. "But you can ride the basket."

They argued about the basket, discovered a wasp nest in it, and fled the garage screaming with laughter, which was apparently a valid ending, because Mr. Jean-Louis clapped three times and said, "Now that is a scene."

Walking out at the end of the day, Maelie could still feel the shape of that bicycle in her hands, red and wobbling and entirely made up. Jaxton jogged up beside her, still grinning.

"Tomorrow," he said, "Grandma's bicycle has a sidecar."

"With room for Ezekiel," said Maelie.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Raw onion tastes sharp, but cooking it slowly over low heat makes it soft and sweet as its natural sugars turn golden brown.
story:
Hazel held the knife the way Ms. Kapoor had shown her, fingers curled inward like a bear paw, knuckles out front.
