"This is the claw grip," Ms. Kapoor said, and demonstrated on her own half onion, the blade sliding down and stopping short of her fingertips. "Curved fingers, slow cuts. The knife respects the knuckle."

Hazel respected it too, mostly because the week before, Mathys had gone fast and lost a sliver of thumbnail, and the community kitchen's first aid kit turned out to be one ancient bandage and a cough drop. She cut her onion into even pieces, eyes streaming so hard she had to step back from the board. Corbin, stationed at the next table, watched from a distance usually reserved for people avoiding a virus.

"I don't eat onions," he announced, as if she'd offered him one.

"You're going to," Hazel said. "It's sauce. Onions are the whole base."

"Then I'll eat around them."

Ms. Kapoor set a wide pan on the stove and turned the flame down low, low enough that it looked almost off. "Slow heat, and don't rush it," she said, and moved on to check someone's garlic, leaving Hazel alone with a pile of pale raw onion bits and a pan that seemed to be doing nothing at all.

Hazel waited. The onions sat there, opaque white and stubborn, and she began to suspect the burner was broken. She tried a piece from the cutting board first, raw, and her whole face cramped; it was sharp enough to make her eyes water a second time, which she felt was unfair. Then she poked at the pan. The onions had gone soft and floppy, and a smell was rising that was warm and almost like toast. She fished one out with the wooden spoon, blew on it, and ate it. It was sweet. Golden, soft, sweet, nothing like the sharp thing she'd chewed thirty seconds ago. She stood there recalculating her entire opinion of onions. Same vegetable. The slow low heat had done that. She took another piece to be sure.

She carried the spoon across the room like evidence at a trial and held it under Corbin's nose. "Raw onion tastes like that." She pointed at the cutting board. "This is what happens when you cook it slow. Different vegetable, practically."

"Absolutely not," Corbin said. He looked at the ceiling, the window, anywhere but the spoon. Then his shoulders did something involuntary, and he leaned in and took the smallest possible bite. He chewed. He chewed again, slower.

"There's sugar in there or something," he said suspiciously.

"There isn't. It's just the onion." Hazel was already walking back to the stove. "Told you."

When the sauce was done, bubbling and dark red over the softened onions, Corbin was first in line with his bowl. He came back twice. The second time, he scraped the bottom of the pot with a piece of bread and said, without looking up, "Does this work on mushrooms too?"

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, objects of the same real size, like lampposts along a street, are drawn smaller and closer together the farther away they are.
story:
Carson had signed up for the art shack at Camp Birchwood mostly because his mother said he couldn't spend another summer indoors, and now he regretted it, because the sheet of paper in front of him showed a street that looked like a flat wall.

"Yours too?" Hunter whispered from the next stool, holding up his own drawing. He had drawn a road running straight back between two rows of lampposts, and every single lamppost was exactly the same height, standing the same distance from its neighbors, like fence posts. The road just stopped being a road.

Mr. Doyle walked between the easels, humming something under his breath. When he reached Hunter's table he paused, tapped the corner of the page, and said only, "Look out the window. Then look at your paper. Then tell me what your eyes know that your hand doesn't." He moved on before Hunter could answer.

Carson looked out the window. Below the art shack, the dirt path ran down toward the lake, and a line of tall wooden light poles marched along the edge of it. The nearest pole was huge, a brown column with a bright lamp on top. The farthest one, way down by the dock, was a stubby little stick, hardly bigger than his thumb at arm's length. He raised his thumb and measured again, walking his gaze back up the line. Pole by pole, each one looked smaller than the one before it, and the gaps between them squeezed tighter and tighter until the last two almost touched.

"Whoa," Carson said. He grabbed a fresh pencil. "Hunter. The poles get smaller the farther away they are."

"That's weird," Hunter said. "They're all the same height in real life. I measured one once."

"That's the point. Same real size, but they look smaller and closer together the farther they go." Carson drew his street again, but this time he made the first lamppost tall as his hand, the next one a little shorter, the next shorter still, and squashed the spaces between them smaller and smaller, until they all shrank down toward one tiny dot near the top of the page where the road vanished. He'd heard Mr. Doyle say the words that morning and hadn't understood them until now. "Vanishing point," he said quietly, almost to himself.

Across the room, Violet leaned over from the still-life table to see what the whispering was about. Her eyebrows went up. "That actually looks like a street," she said. "Like you could walk down it."

Hunter was already erasing his lampposts, tongue poking out the corner of his mouth, shrinking each one row by row. When Mr. Doyle came back around, he stopped at Hunter's table for a long moment and said nothing at all, which Carson was starting to understand was the highest praise the man handed out.

Mr. Doyle set a real challenge on the table before the afternoon was over. The camp director wanted a poster of Main Street for the talent show on Friday, and the three of them would paint it together, buildings and lampposts and all. It would take the rest of the week.

Outside the window, a flock of geese crossed the sky over the lake, the first migratory birds of the season heading south in a long wobbling V. Violet pointed at them and laughed because the V, seen from the side, looked like their street, everything bunched toward a faraway point.

"There's a high probability we ruin the poster," Hunter said, shading another shrinking lamppost.

"There's a probability we don't," Carson said, and picked up his pencil to add a mailbox, small, smaller, smallest, marching down toward the dot.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: The 800 metres draws on aerobic energy, which uses oxygen, and anaerobic energy, which works without oxygen but runs out quickly, so it feels like a sprint and a distance race at once.
story:
Owen stood at the starting line of the school track with Bronwyn on his right and Kai on his left. All three of them had signed up for the eight hundred metres for the first time, and Mr. Weiss had given them exactly one instruction: "Save something for the second lap."

Bronwyn laughed. She won every hundred-metre sprint in the district. "Save something? I have plenty." The gun went off, and she was gone, two lanes ahead before the first curve. Kai, who ran cross-country every fall, settled into a smooth, even rhythm beside Owen, and the two of them ran nearly parallel down the backstretch. Owen wanted to chase Bronwyn, but he had a theory. She was sprinting like the race was short, and something about the way she'd gone out made him suspicious.

"The eight hundred is weird," Kai puffed between breaths. "It's like two races glued together. Mr. Weiss says it draws on aerobic energy, that's the kind with oxygen, and anaerobic energy. That kind works without oxygen, but it runs out fast. So it feels like a sprint and a distance race at the same time."

"That's a paradox," Owen said.

"Feels more like a trap," Kai said.

They crossed the first lap with Bronwyn ten metres ahead, arms still pumping. Then the trap sprang. Her stride shortened. Her shoulders rose. By the far curve she was drifting sideways as tiredness invaded her legs, and Owen and Kai went past her one after the other. Owen counted his own breathing, kept his pace even, and held his kick for the last hundred. He finished first, one second ahead of Kai, and bent over with his hands on his knees.

Bronwyn stumbled in thirty seconds later and dropped onto the infield grass. "That race is broken," she announced. "Somebody should fix it."

Mr. Weiss walked over with his clipboard and looked down at her. "The race is fine, Bronwyn. The pacing was broken."

Owen sat down beside her, still catching his breath. Bronwyn glared at the finish line. "Next meet," she said, "I'm running the first lap easy. And then I'm going to sprint the whole second one, and I'm going to win."

"You'll run out again," Kai said from the other side, unwrapping an orange.

Bronwyn folded her arms. "Then I'll sprint half of it. I'll do the math tonight."

Owen watched her get up and walk toward the water fountain, already muttering numbers to herself. Mr. Weiss wrote something on his clipboard and turned toward the next heat. "Lane three," he called. "You're up."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about something that will happen later, often noticed only on a second reading.
story:
Megan sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with the short story "The Winter Road" spread in front of her and a pencil behind her ear. Tomorrow in Mr. Khan's class everyone had to point out one example of foreshadowing or symbolism and explain what it suggested, and Megan had read the story twice and still had nothing. Lyanna had already claimed the river, which froze solid in the first paragraph and cracked at the end, obviously standing for something. Harrison had texted Megan a whole list of ideas, but Megan suspected he had copied them off the internet, which Mr. Khan would sniff out instantly.

"You're overcomplicating it," Lyanna said from Megan's bed, where she was supposed to be doing her own reading for the assignment. She had her own reason for being there: she wanted Megan to promise they would present together on Thursday, so their grades would be linked and Lyanna's would look stronger. "Just take the crow. The crow is obviously a symbol. Birds mean death in every movie ever."

"I don't want obvious," Megan said. "I want the thing nobody else saw." She flipped back to page one, mostly to avoid Lyanna's eyes, and started reading again even though she'd sworn she was done. The main character, a girl walking to her grandmother's house, stopped to check a loose board in the footbridge. That was it. One sentence. The girl pressed the board with her toe, decided it would hold, and walked on.

Megan sat up so fast the pencil fell out from behind her ear. The bridge. At the end of the story, the girl crossed that same bridge in the dark, running, and the board gave way. On her first read she had sailed right past that early sentence, but now it looked like a lit match in a dark room. She checked the page number of the bridge scene twice, then once more, because she did not want to be the kid who stood up in class and got the whole thing wrong.

"Listen to this," Megan said, and read the sentence aloud. "The clue was sitting there on page one the whole time. Mr. Khan said foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about something that happens later, and you usually only catch it on a second reading. That's exactly what just happened to me. First time through, nothing. Second time, there it is."

Lyanna put down her book. "Okay, that's better than my crow," she admitted. "So we present together and you lead with the bridge." Megan hesitated, because half of her wanted to say no and keep the discovery to herself. But Lyanna was leaning forward now, genuinely scribbling notes, the way she did when she actually cared, and Megan changed her mind mid-breath. "Fine," she said. "But you do the symbolism part. Your crow is actually competent, if you cut the part about movies." Lyanna grinned and started a fresh page of notes, and Megan flipped back to page one and read the sentence about the loose board one more time, underlining it slowly, twice.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
Harper sat cross-legged on Kiara's bedroom floor with Kiara's phone balanced on a stack of graphic novels, while her own phone sat in her lap like a guilty dog. "He actually typed it in all caps?" she asked.

"Every word," Kiara said. "Kasey screenshotted it. Mr. Santoso's message said, 'REMEMBER, THE GROUP CHAT IS FOR HOMEWORK ONLY.' And then twenty people replied with crying-laughing faces, which honestly made it worse."

The class chat was three days old and already a disaster. Someone had posted a video of a cat, then someone else had posted forty links to a game, and then the argument started about whether exclamation points meant you were yelling or just friendly. Harper scrolled through the screenshots Kiara had saved, trying to scrutinize the messages for some hidden rule, some pattern that separated the posts that got laughs from the posts that got people mad. All-caps from Mr. Santoso felt like yelling. All-caps from Kasey felt like a bit. Same letters, different feeling. That made no sense, and Harper wanted it to make sense.

She remembered sixth grade, before anyone had group chats, when she'd passed a folded note to Kiara in math class. The note said something joking about their teacher's tie, and Kiara had laughed out loud right in the middle of a quiz, and they'd both gotten detention. A note was private until it wasn't. A chat felt like the same thing, except a hundred times worse, because the note could only be stolen by one person.

"We need actual rules," Harper said. "Like, written-down rules. But who writes rules for typing?"

"Nobody writes rules for typing," Kiara said. "It's just... typing."

Harper doubted that. Somebody wrote rules for everything, even library whispering and swimming pool walking. She searched on her phone: rules for communicating online. Then: official online manners. Then, feeling a little ridiculous: were there ever official rules for the internet. A result came up that looked like homework from 1995, dry as toast, called RFC 1855.

"Wait," Harper said. "There's a whole thing. One of the first written guides to online manners was published in 1995, and it's a document called RFC 1855."

"RFC like a soccer thing?"

"Like a boring thing. Netiquette Guidelines. Somebody sat down and wrote rules like a legend."

Kiara leaned over her shoulder. "1995. That's before my parents even had a computer."

Harper scrolled. Rule after rule about tone, about not assuming the reader can hear your voice, about public messages versus private ones. It was like someone had read the inside of her head and published it decades before she was born. "So caps from Kasey is a joke because we know Kasey, and caps from Mr. Santoso is a lecture because he's the teacher," she said. "Same public message, different private feelings. The rules were there the whole time, we just never wrote them."

They drafted a list for the class chat: caps only for comedy, homework stuff in the daytime, cat videos allowed on Fridays. Kiara typed it up and read it aloud in her most eloquent news-anchor voice, which cracked them both up. They posted it, signed with both their names.

The twist came at nine o'clock. Mr. Santoso replied in the chat, in careful lowercase: "thank you for this. my daughter suggested the caps lock. I told her teachers need to seem serious. she says I seem like a toaster." Then a single cat emoji.

Harper stared at the screen. "He has a daughter?"

"Two more replies just came in," Kiara said. "Look. He signed one of them RFC 1855."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
The farewell party was in full swing in Carter's backyard, which meant that Ryann had already eaten three cupcakes and Jude was trying to win the piñata even though there was no blindfold and no rules. Carter sat on the porch steps beside a kid named, well, a kid whose name Carter honestly could not remember, which was awkward because the kid had come specifically to see him.

"I moved here two weeks ago," the kid said. "My mom said you're the one leaving, so we should hang out before you go."

Carter did the math in his head. Two weeks, one shared lunch period, one group project where they had mostly passed glue sticks. That was maybe four hours total. Something about that bothered him, like a splinter he couldn't see.

Ryann flopped down beside them, cupcake number four in hand. "What's with the face, Carter? You look like you're doing long division."

"I read this thing online," Carter said slowly, testing it out loud. "A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend."

"Fifty hours," the kid repeated. "That's a lot of hours."

"That's why!" Carter sat up. "That's why it feels weird. You and me, we've got maybe four hours logged. We're basically strangers with excellent glue stick teamwork." He pulled out his phone and opened the calculator, which felt very official. "If we played video games for two hours a night, that's twenty-five nights. But I'm moving Saturday."

"Road trip," the kid offered. "If your new town is four hours away, and my mom drives me there twelve times, and I drive back twelve times..."

"You can't drive."

"It's a plan for later."

Jude abandoned the piñata, which had survived everything, and stomped over holding Carter's telescope like a shield. "Okay, party's over for me unless someone addresses the elephant." He thrust the telescope forward. "You're leaving this here. With me. On purpose. And every time I look at the moon I'll envy whoever's looking at it with you in your fancy new town with your fancy new friends." His voice cracked on "friends," and he pretended it hadn't.

"You already have fifty hours with me," Carter said. "Probably three hundred. You're safe. You're the most casual friend I have."

Jude sniffled and aimed the telescope at the piñata. "It does have a warranty, right? If I drop it?"

"It's a telescope, not a toaster. And stop pointing it at the piñata, that's invasive. It's been through enough."

The kid raised his hand like he was in class. "Question. If I get my fifty hours with Carter before he moves, do I get the piñata?"

"It's not mine to give, but yes," Carter said, and they all turned to look at it, hanging there, smug and unbroken, and Ryann went to get the broom handle.

knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: A pivot table's summary can be switched from Sum or Count to Average, turning a column of one-to-five ratings into the mean rating for each grade.
story:
Lillian clicked through the survey results for the third time and frowned at the screen. Three hundred twelve students had answered the question "How much did you like the fall field trip to the science museum, one to five?", and every answer sat in one long column of numbers that told her nothing.

"You're still on that?" Devyn asked from the next computer. "Just count the fives and be done."

"Counting fives is naive," Lillian said. "The eights who hated it matter too."

Mr. Anderson, walking between the rows of monitors, paused behind her. "Pivot table," he said, tapping her screen once. "Values, rows, and it's under Insert." Then he moved on before she could ask what any of that meant.

She dragged the grade column into Rows, and the spreadsheet folded itself into six neat lines: sixth, seventh, eighth, plus three grades that did not exist, which she deleted. She dragged the rating column into Values and got counts. Big numbers. Useless numbers. She remembered last spring, when she had tallied the book fair survey by hand on paper, one tally mark at a time for two evenings, and had still gotten the seventh grade wrong. She had opposed doing it digitally back then because she thought spreadsheets were for business people, not for someone who just wanted to know whether kids liked pizza day. That choice felt foolish now, sitting in the computer lab with the whole answer one click away.

She right-clicked the count and a menu appeared. Sum. Count. Average. She chose Sum first, because the ratings were numbers, so adding them seemed natural. The spreadsheet gave her totals in the hundreds. Interesting, but not an answer. Then she tried Average.

The numbers changed to small decimals. Sixth grade: 4.6. Seventh: 4.2. Eighth: 3.1. She sat back. "Devyn. The eighth graders liked it way less."

Devyn leaned over. "Wait, how'd you get that? That's not counting anything."

"The average," Lillian said. "Instead of Sum or Count, you switch it to Average. So a column of one-to-five ratings turns into the mean rating for each grade."

"That's it? That's the whole trick?"

Lillian looked at the 3.1 glowing beside Eighth Grade, and thought about her older sister, who had complained the whole bus ride home about the crowds and the boring mineral exhibit. She thought about last spring's paper tallies, about how she had reported the seventh grade's favorite when it probably had not been. Should she have known to ask more than "who picked five"? She did not decide. She printed the pivot table instead.

"Mr. Anderson," she called across the lab, holding up the page. "The eighth graders rated the trip 3.1. What do we do with that?"

He took the sheet and looked at it for a long moment. "That," he said, "is the frontier. Everything past the count is where it gets interesting."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters" can push readers toward opposite opinions.
story:
The science fair project was due Monday, and Victoria still needed a poster board, which was why she was at the mall on Saturday with Leonard and Seerat instead of anywhere fun. The supply store closed at six, and it was already quarter past five, but the three of them kept stopping, because the mall was full of screens, and the screens kept shouting at them.

"Everyone's switching," boomed a voice over the shoe store's speaker, above a wall of glowing sneakers. "Join the millions who already know." Victoria slowed down. She counted four different signs saying almost the same thing. Millions, everyone, everybody. Why did the store care whether she thought other people had bought the shoes? She nudged Seerat. "Do you actually want those, or do you just feel like you're the last person on earth without them?" Seerat grinned and kept walking, but Victoria filed the question away, the way she filed things for their class news project.

That project was the real deadline underneath the poster deadline. Mr. Yilmaz had assigned it Friday: find two articles about the same event and present them Monday. Victoria had both headlines saved on her phone, and in the food court, waiting for Leonard to finish his pretzel, she slid the phone across the table. "Same rally, same day, same city," she said. "Look." The first headline called the crowd protesters. The second called the exact same crowd rioters. She watched Seerat's face change as she read each one, falling forward, then hardening. "They're describing the same people," Seerat said slowly. "But I feel completely different about them depending which one I read."

"So that's the poster," Victoria said, her heart going quick. "Same crowd, two words, opposite opinions." It was like the sneaker signs, but sharper. The shoe store had leaned on her with everybody-else-is-doing-it, and the famous athlete grinning from the sunglasses kiosk had leaned on her too, though she'd never once wondered whether he actually wore those sunglasses. The news headlines did something else: they slipped a feeling inside a single word and let it do the pushing. She wondered how many words worked like that, quiet and invisible, like a parasite riding along on a sentence.

At five to six they ran for the supply store, and at the register the cashier pointed at the poster racks. "The foam ones are on sale today only. And laminating is mandatory on the sale price, just so you know." Victoria squinted at the sign. Mandatory was a strong word for something the store simply wanted, and "today only" made her pulse hurry in a way she didn't like being told to feel. She bought the plain board at the regular price, skipped the laminate, and saved four dollars.

Outside, Leonard balancing the rolled-up board under his arm, Victoria said, "Monday, we put both headlines side by side and don't say a word. We just let the class read them." Seerat was already typing the title. "Two Words, Two Opinions," she said.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Layla slid into the booth beside her dad, who was already pointing at the third TV over the bar. "Four hundred metres final," he said. "Replay starts in a minute." Her little brother was busy stacking coasters, and her mom flagged down a waiter to order nachos for the table, since Layla had skipped lunch after her tedious morning of standardized testing.

On the screen, eight runners settled into their blocks. Layla recognized the favourite, a runner in lane four, because his face was on half the posters at school. "He's ranked first in the world," her dad said. "That means he's basically unbeatable."

Layla frowned at that. She had spent the whole week in math class on averages and percentages, and something about "first in the world" bothered her. "Ranked first," she said slowly, "but first by how much?"

"Does it matter?" her dad asked. "First is first."

The gun fired and the bar went quiet except for the fryer. Down the backstretch the runner in lane six, silver-bibbed, crept up on the favourite until they were nearly even. Around the final bend Layla was on her knees on the booth's bench, and half the bar was yelling. The two leaders hit the line together, so close that Layla couldn't tell who won until the replay froze on the finish and zoomed in.

"Second by four hundredths of a second," the announcer said. The silver medalist had lost by less time than a blink. Layla's dad exhaled like he'd been holding his breath the whole race.

"See?" Layla said. "Ranking first doesn't tell you the distance. That guy was first and second was practically on top of him. But first and second could also be a whole minute apart if the race was lopsided, and it would still just say first and second." She assumed everyone at the table would shrug, but her little brother looked up from his coasters.

"So the medal doesn't say how close it was?"

"Exactly. It just says the order." She pulled a napkin and drew two stick figures crossing a line, then wrote "1st" and "2nd" with a tiny gap between them, and beside it drew the same two figures with a huge gap. "Same ranking, totally different race."

Her dad turned his glass slowly. "So when I tell people the favourite always wins, that's a bad premise."

"A shaky one," Layla said, grinning.

Mr. Bautista, their neighbour from two doors down, leaned over from the next booth with his basket of wings. "You just explained why I never trust the sports ticker," he said. "My granddaughter argues the same way. Can I steal that napkin?"

Layla added two more stick figures and slid it across the table to him.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end.
story:
The bus lurched around the corner by the hardware store, and Mason slid down the seat so he wouldn't have to look at Jersey, who was sitting three rows up with the soccer kids. It hadn't always been like this. In sixth grade they'd shared a bench every single morning, arguing about whose turn it was to hold the granola bars. Then Mason joined the robotics club and Jersey made the travel team, and somehow they'd stopped talking about anything that mattered.

Mason kept turning the problem over, the way he turned over a stuck gear in his head. Robots followed rules you could test. If a motor wouldn't spin, you checked the battery, then the wires, then the piston in the little air pump that refused to move. You didn't guess. You tried one thing at a time. So what had broken between him and Jersey? He decided to run a test, to simulate a normal conversation and see what happened.

He waited until the bus hit the long straight stretch past the creek, then moved up and dropped into the seat beside Jersey. "Hey," he said. "Did you see that penalty kick Saturday?" Jersey lit up for a second, and they talked about the game for two stops. Then Mason tried the second half of his test. "Also, my robot finally pushed the block across the table yesterday." Jersey nodded, said "cool," and looked out the window. The pattern was clear. They could still talk about Jersey's stuff. Mason's stuff had gone silent.

Zariah, who rode from the last stop and saw everything, leaned across the aisle. "You two used to be glued together," she said. "What happened?" Mason shrugged. "Different teams, I guess." Zariah pulled out her phone. "We read about this in Mr. Petrov's class. A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end." She scrolled to the page and held it out so he could see it was real.

Mason stared at the sentence. He'd been testing wires and batteries when the actual problem was the whole circuit. It wasn't that Jersey was mad. It was that they'd grown into two different shapes that didn't fit together anymore, unless one of them changed shape a little. He couldn't make himself love soccer, and he couldn't make Jersey love robots. But maybe the fit didn't have to be identical. Maybe it just had to overlap somewhere new.

"Zariah," he said slowly, "what do you actually care about? Like your thing." She grinned. "Statistical stuff, honestly. I made a chart of every free throw our girls' team took last season." Mason's brain sparked like a loose connection snapping back into place. "Wait. I need numbers for my robot. Timing data, distances, everything. And Jersey collects stats for his team in a notebook. All three of us could measure stuff."

He leaned forward and tapped Jersey's shoulder. "You know how you write down every shot your team takes? I want to build something that reads those numbers and predicts the next play. Zariah can check whether it actually works. You in?" Jersey turned around, and for the first time in weeks his whole face was interested. "You could do that with my notebook? For real?"

"I need somebody who knows what the numbers mean," Mason said. "That's you." Jersey grabbed his backpack, unzipped the front pocket, and pulled out the battered green notebook, already flipping it open to a page of neatly boxed scores. "Start with Tuesday," he said. "We took forty-one shots."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported.
story:
The lights went out at 7:40, right in the middle of Connor's homework, and the refrigerator stopped its humming for the first time in his whole life. He heard his mom feel her way to the junk drawer, then a flashlight clicked on. "Candle," she said. "And find the old board games, because this is going to be a while."

Connor sat on the kitchen floor with the flashlight and thought. The whole street was dark; he could see that from the window. On his way home from school, after the storm, Tianna and Monica had stopped dead at the corner of Maple and Third, where a black wire lay across the sidewalk. It wasn't sparking or buzzing or doing anything dramatic. It just lay there, wet and ordinary. Monica had reached toward it, and Tianna had grabbed her sleeve. "Don't," Tianna said. "A fallen line can still be live even when it isn't sparking. My dad says you treat it like it's on, you stay way back, and you tell someone." They had gone the long way around and told Mr. Nakamura, who was out checking his fence. He had thanked them seriously and gone inside to phone it in.

Now Connor formulated a plan. If that wire was the reason the street was dark, then calling the power company's emergency line and telling them exactly where the line was might speed things up. He borrowed his mom's phone, gave the recorded voice the address, and a real person came on. "Yes, we have a crew dispatched to that location," she said. "Tell everyone to stay well away from it."

"There's nothing well away about it," said his sister from the stairs. "It's on the sidewalk where everyone walks to school."

"Then tomorrow morning we put a garbage can on each end of the block," Connor said. "Away from the wire. And we stand there and tell people until the truck comes."

The lights came back at 9:15, all at once, so bright that everyone in the kitchen winced. The freezer shuddered and started up, saving the pierogi his grandmother had taught his mom to make, dough and all, a heritage that went back three kitchens and two countries. Connor's mom declared the rescue of the pierogi a triumph. "Power outages are inevitable in a storm," she said, "but losing dinner is not."

The next morning the wire was gone. Connor, Tianna, and Monica walked the long way anyway, just to check, and Monica kicked a pebble the entire length of Maple Street.

"Next time it storms," she said, "I'm walking with my hands in my pockets."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The Japanese word origami comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper.
story:
The paper crane collapsed in Arianna's hands for the fourth time, its wings flopping sideways like a bird that had given up on flying. Across the long table at the community art studio, Harleen held up a crane so crisp it could probably cut you.

"Maybe you just need better paper," Harleen suggested.

Arianna didn't think that was it. She was using the same square of silvery foil paper as Harleen, and her folds had been sharp at first. The trouble started partway through, when the model reached a kind of plateau and stopped improving no matter how many times she creased and uncreased. Something invisible was going wrong, and she wanted to know what. She smoothed the failed crane flat and studied the sheet, turning it over, holding it up to the window light.

"Try it with the paper turned the other way," said Leah, who was across the table struggling with a frog. "Like, rotate it ninety degrees before you start."

"You think the paper has a direction?" Arianna asked.

"Paper's made in sheets going one way," Leah said with a shrug. "My grandpa prints stuff and he complains about it constantly. It's like wood. It wants to bend one way and not the other."

Arianna looked at her crease marks. Every fold she'd made across the sheet had come out clean, and every fold down its length had turned mushy and thick. That was a pattern, and patterns meant something. She cut a fresh square from the same sheet of foil paper, rotated it a quarter turn, and began again, creasing slowly and testing each fold before committing to the next one. The sideways folds, the ones that had refused before, slid into place like they'd been waiting for her.

While she worked, Harleen leaned over. "Did you know the word origami isn't about beauty or anything? It means fold and paper. 'Ori' means to fold, and 'kami' means paper." She tapped Arianna's crooked first crane. "So the word literally just describes what you're doing. Folding paper. No magic in it."

"So the magic has to come from somewhere else," Arianna said. "Like direction. Which nobody named in the word." She laughed. "Origami means folding paper, and apparently the paper still gets a vote."

Ms. Ong, the studio's teacher, wandered past with a tray of glue sticks and paused over the half-finished crane. "That one's behaving," she observed.

"It's the same paper as before," Arianna said. "I just turned it."

By the end of the session, Arianna's crane stood on the table with wings that snapped open when she pulled the tail. Leah's frog still looked barren and defeated, a flat green nothing with legs pointing in four directions. Arianna slid her leftover foil paper across the table, turned it a quarter turn, and set it in front of her friend.

"Rotate first," she said. "Then fold."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A formula that includes its own cell, such as =SUM(B2:B10) typed into cell B10, is called a circular reference, and Excel warns about it.
story:
The laptop cart in Room 12 was so dilapidated that Ms. Das had to jiggle the hinge of every machine just to make the screens stay open. Gabriella grabbed the one with the least cracked casing and carried it to the table beside Sandra, who was already tapping away at hers. They had forty minutes before the talent show auditions at lunch, and Gabriella needed a bar chart of the fundraiser totals for her proposal to Ms. Das. Each row of the spreadsheet held a day of the bake sale, and column B held the money collected. All she had to do was add it up.

"Ms. Das prohibits food in here, so don't bring your audition muffin," Sandra said without looking up. "I'm serious, she confiscated a granola bar on Tuesday."

"I'm not risking my muffin," Gabriella said. She typed the day totals into B2 through B10, nine days of quarters and crumpled dollars. Then, in the very last box of the column, B10, she wrote the total formula, =SUM(B2:B10), because it seemed tidy to keep the answer at the bottom of the list. She pressed Enter and a gray warning box popped onto the screen. Circular reference, it said. She read the words twice. What was circling? Nothing on the screen was moving.

She leaned closer, wondering if the formula was somehow pointing at itself. It included B10, and she had typed it into B10. Was the sum trying to add up its own answer? She decided to test it the simple way: she copied the formula, deleted it from B10, and pasted it into B11, one row below the column. The total appeared instantly, 143 dollars and 75 cents, and the warning vanished. So that was the rule. She hadn't known it had a name until Sandra glanced over and said, "Oh, a circular reference. My brother got that last year."

"That's what it's called?" Gabriella said. "A circular reference."

"Circular reference," Ms. Das confirmed as she walked past, tapping the side of the warning box on Mathis's screen down the row, where the same gray message had appeared. "Move it out of the column, everyone, and check your totals." Mathis groaned and slid his formula down one row, and his sum sprang to life too.

Gabriella highlighted her column, clicked the chart button, and watched nine bars rise across the screen, Tuesday towering over every other day. The lunch bell rang before she could admire it for long. She saved the file, closed the dilapidated laptop, and tucked her muffin deep into her backpack where nobody could confiscate anything. "Coming to the auditions?" Sandra asked, already at the door. "After I show Ms. Das my chart," Gabriella said, and held the screen open one more second so the tallest bar caught the light.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: In German, every noun begins with a capital letter, so "I have a dog and a cat" is written "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze."
story:
Brielle slid her laptop across the table so Evelina could see the screen. Red squiggles ran through her German paragraph like scratches, under "hund," under "katze," under "schwester," even under her own name. "I typed it the way I say it," she said. "The spell-checker hates everything."

Ms. De Vries leaned over from the next desk, but she only said, "Look closely at what the checker circles. Count them." Then she moved on to help Elsie, whose screen was almost as red.

Brielle stared until her eyes ached. The checker had not flagged "ich," or "habe," or "und," or "ein." She began to isolate the marked words, dragging each one into a list at the bottom of her document. Hund. Katze. Schwester. Mutter. Vater. Then she made a second list of the unmarked ones: ich, habe, und, ist, meine. She read both columns twice, and her pencil tapped faster and faster.

"Evelina," she whispered. "Every word it circles is a thing. A noun. Hund, cat, sister, mother. All the nouns." She opened a fresh line and typed, "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," giving each noun a capital letter at the start. The red vanished, one squiggle at a time, like frost melting off a window. She grinned so wide her cheeks hurt. Her paragraph about her family had looked impoverished before, all errors and no real sentences, but now it said what she meant: that she had a dog named after a baker, a cat who ignored everyone, and a little sister who talked nonstop.

She reached over to Elsie's laptop without being asked. "Try capitals on your nouns," Brielle said. "Watch." She typed "Meine Familie" and the checker stayed silent. Elsie copied the idea, fixing her whole first paragraph while Evelina read hers aloud, halting but real: "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze." When she finished, she looked up, out of breath, and Brielle clapped twice, quiet and fast, so only their table could hear.

At the end of class, Ms. De Vries collected the laptops. "Yours is the only one with no red left," she said to Brielle, and slid it into the cart with the screen still showing the line, "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," every noun tall and gleaming at the front.
